Getting started with clutchserve

library(clutchserve)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

Do the greats really serve better when it matters most?

Commentators love calling the great players “clutch”. This package puts that to the test. It compares how often a player wins pressure points on their own serve with how often they win every other service point. Intuitively, most players’ level drops a little under pressure, so the real question is: who drops less than a typical player?

This guide shows how to install the package, launch the app, use its controls, and read what it shows.

Install

The source code is on GitHub.

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-pang0023-arch")

Launch the app 

clutchserve::run_app()

The app opens in your browser. Everything it shows comes from the serve_pressure dataset included in the package.

Use the controls

The sidebar has four controls. Each one changes which players and points are included:

  1. Surface: Filter matches on hard, clay, grass courts, or keep all selected for an overview.
  2. Years: Filter matches to a range of years (1990 onwards).
  3. What counts as a pressure point?: Break points only: points where the server is one point from losing the game. Break points and deuce: also counts points at 40–40.
  4. Minimum pressure points per player: Hide players with too few pressure points. A higher minimum leaves fewer players, but their results are more reliable.

If the settings leave too few players, or no surface is ticked, the app explains what went wrong and how to fix it instead of showing an empty chart.

Read the main chart (funnel chart)

Each dot is a player.

  • x-axis: how many pressure points the player faced (log scale).
  • y-axis: the player’s pressure-point drop compared with a typical player. Above 0 means they drop less than typical under pressure (more clutch); below 0 means they drop more.
  • Shaded band: the range a typical player’s result would usually fall in. It narrows to the right, because with more points the result reflects skill more than luck.
  • Colours: teal dots are above the band (more clutch than typical), coral dots are below it (less clutch), and grey dots are within normal variation.

Hover over a dot to see the player’s numbers. Click a dot to follow that player in the chart below.

Read the player chart

The second chart shows one player year by year:

  • Dark green line: share of pressure points won.
  • Light green line: share of other service points won.
  • Dot size: how many pressure points that year. Big dots are reliable; small dots can swing a lot by chance.

The closer the dark line is to the light line, the less pressure affects the player. Look at the overall pattern rather than single years.

How the comparison works

The app uses pressure_gap(), which you can also use yourself. It gives one row per player:

players <- pressure_gap(serve_pressure) |>
  filter(reliable)

players |>
  select(player, pressure_pts, pressure_pct, other_pct, gap) |>
  head()
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   player          pressure_pts pressure_pct other_pct     gap
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Roger Federer           3437        0.659     0.695 -0.0354
#> 2 Novak Djokovic          3119        0.640     0.671 -0.0311
#> 3 Rafael Nadal            2598        0.639     0.661 -0.0226
#> 4 Andy Murray             1810        0.604     0.639 -0.0347
#> 5 Hubert Hurkacz          1624        0.666     0.683 -0.0171
#> 6 Daniil Medvedev         1579        0.631     0.663 -0.0317
  • pressure_pct: share of pressure points won
  • other_pct: share of other service points won
  • gap: pressure_pct minus other_pct. A negative gap means the player wins fewer pressure points than other points.

The app then compares each player’s gap with the typical (median) gap:

typical_gap <- median(players$gap)
typical_pct <- median(players$pressure_pct)

players <- players |>
  mutate(
    vs_typical = gap - typical_gap,
    luck_limit = 1.96 * sqrt(typical_pct * (1 - typical_pct) / pressure_pts),
    verdict = case_when(
      vs_typical >  luck_limit ~ "More clutch than typical",
      vs_typical < -luck_limit ~ "Less clutch than typical",
      TRUE                     ~ "Within normal variation"
    )
  )

With the default settings, 201 players have at least 100 pressure points. A typical player wins 2.3 percentage points fewer of their pressure points than of their other service points.

The luck_limit is the half-width of the shaded band: 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) / n), where p is the typical share of pressure points won and n is the player’s number of pressure points.

A dot outside the band is likely a combination of skill and luck: the result is bigger than luck alone would usually produce, but with about 200 players, around 10 would land outside a 95% band by chance anyway. So treat players outside the band as worth a closer look, not as proof they are clutch.

Limitations

  • Not a random sample. Volunteers chart the matches they choose, so famous players and big matches are overrepresented. Results describe the charted matches, not every match a player has played.
  • Opponent strength is ignored. A break point against a great returner is harder to win, and top players often face each other in the matches that get charted.
  • Serving is only half the story. The package only looks at points on a player’s own serve, not how they return.
